<reason>A won a close, high-quality exchange by staying on the motion’s science-per-dollar test: unique crew advantages were admitted, then weighed against recurring life-support and architecture costs rather than treated as a majority entitlement. B’s best live route—lumpy industrial base plus unique field science—was sticky and well-phrased, but never showed why preservation requires most of the budget, and B made the comparison hard to lose by folding presence into “science.” A’s pressure on majority-versus-preservation, plus the turn that high fixed costs strengthen selection rather than create a blank check, decided the clash.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A’s R2/closing turn of B’s architecture claim: crew skills count, but charging the whole standing system against forgone robotic discovery means high fixed costs demand selection, not “fund the majority or lose the option.”</best_rebuttal>
